#9735. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

#9734. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

#9733. Node.js Delayed Queue Processing: Smoothing US/EU Webhook Spikes Within Rate Limits

Retries improve the chance that a shipment notification arrives, but they also create another opportunity to apply the same delivery twice. Resolve that trade-off at the receiver: persist a stable business-event identity before acknowledging successful processing. TL;DR: use a managed delayed queue to smooth rate-limited outbound work when delays fit within seven days and consumers tolerate at-least-once delivery. Pair it with durable consumer idempotency. A delayed message alone cannot promise a single business effect.

For a Node.js logistics backend, the decision concerns both correctness and evidence. Queue depth tells an operator whether dispatch is falling behind; a business-event record tells the receiver whether a shipment update has already taken effect. Mixing those responsibilities produces expensive logs and weak guarantees. The useful comparison between QStash, Amazon SQS delay queues, Google Cloud Tasks, and a Redis queue starts with that distinction.

The sender cannot infer the receiver's business state from a missing acknowledgment.

A timeout can mean that processing never started, that it remains in progress, or that processing finished and the reply disappeared. These are design cases, not reported incidents. Retrying is reasonable in all three cases only if repeating the operation is safe.

A shipment event and a delivery attempt need different identities. As a proposed application convention, one shipment status transition retains its event identity across retries, while each attempt gets a separate trace reference. Scope the receiver's uniqueness rule to the intended business effect: a notification for one partner must not suppress a different partner's legitimate notification. The receiver should couple the idempotency record and the business mutation in one atomic operation where its storage supports that arrangement. If an external side effect sits outside that transaction, its own idempotency contract remains necessary; a local success flag cannot make a remote operation atomic.

The queue's deduplication window answers a narrower question. For the managed queue considered here, FIFO deduplication lasts five minutes, whereas standard delivery is at least once. Neither fact removes the consumer's obligation. Retrying an older event can fall outside a broker's window, and deleting a message after acknowledgment does not create an independent archive of the shipment's business history.

Choose the application's idempotency-record lifetime from the longest permitted retry and recovery interval. A seven-day delay allowance does not establish that lifetime by itself. Repeated delays and operational recovery may extend the period during which the same event returns. Retaining the record longer strengthens duplicate protection, but also increases stored state and the time for which business identifiers remain available. That is a deliberate retention decision.

Delay controls eligibility; a dispatch budget controls how much eligible work proceeds. Without a native debounce or throttle primitive, spreading timestamps does not prove that a burst will respect a partner's processing limit. The application needs an explicit policy for eligible attempts, retry timing, and concurrent work. Monitor backlog alongside completed work to check that the chosen budget actually drains the queue.

Consider an illustrative planning case, not a benchmark: 12,000 shipment events arrive together, and a partner permits 20 attempts per second. With no retries or new arrivals, the dispatch floor is 600 seconds. Every retry consumes another attempt from that same budget. If incoming work persistently exceeds completed work, increasing retention postpones expiration but does not solve the capacity deficit.

That arithmetic should shape telemetry too.

Suppose this hypothetical workload generates 100,000 attempts per day and each retained attempt record occupies 1 KB. Seven days requires roughly 700 MB before indexes, replicas, and storage overhead; 30 days requires roughly 3 GB under the same decimal-unit assumption. These are sizing examples, not measurements of any service. Keeping every response body can invalidate the estimate immediately.

Count label combinations before enabling a metric. Under an explicitly hypothetical label set, 2 regions, 4 partner classes, 3 outcomes, and 5 retry buckets permit 120 combinations. Adding an event identifier with 100,000 distinct values permits up to 12 million combinations. Actual occupancy depends on which combinations occur, but the identifier still creates an unbounded growth dimension. Keep event and shipment identities in selectively retained diagnostic records rather than ordinary aggregate metric labels.

Sampling has a correctness boundary. Successful-attempt traces may be sampled for diagnosis, accepting reduced visibility into rare successful paths. Consumer idempotency records must remain complete throughout the chosen protection interval. Failure records deserve a separately bounded retention policy, since retaining every retry forever turns a troubled partner into a storage-growth mechanism. Even error responses can contain shipment data; collect the fields required to resolve an attempt rather than treating the entire body as evidence by default.

Use the following as a selection framework. Regional suitability, dispatch controls, retry configuration, and retention must be checked for the actual deployment; a product name alone is not evidence of US or EU placement. The linked documentation is the starting point for that verification.

These choices are not interchangeable scheduling libraries. A team already operating workers may reasonably prefer a consumption-oriented design; another may value managed HTTP dispatch enough to accept its endpoint and operational requirements. The receiver's duplicate-protection rule remains the same in either case.

Infrai offers 295 routes across 20 modules through one REST API and a single API key. For shipment retries and notification email, the scheduler and mailer share that credential, so the worker does not need another service's key injected when email is added. Its per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata also supports attribution of retry activity without retaining every payload. The combined approach concentrates trust, billing, and outage exposure in one vendor.

For that option, make the limits part of the design: delayed messages support at most seven days, message bodies at most 256 KB, and retention at most 30 days. Acknowledgment deletes the message; there is no Kafka-style replay or multiple-consumer-group history. Public HTTPS is required for push subscriptions, which makes pull consumption attractive for internal workers. Independent pipelines need separate queues because there is no topic-style one-publish-to-many delivery. Workflow DAGs and fan-out joins require another orchestration design.

A logistics retry pipeline may also notify an operator by email after an application-defined terminal decision. That email is another business effect. Give it its own durable identity derived from the shipment event and notification purpose; replaying a webhook attempt must not create another operator notification merely because the worker restarted.

The handoff requires an adapter. The queue consumer receives a job, checks the receiver outcome, and constructs the email batch request only when the notification policy calls for it. Do not post an entire queue response directly to a mail endpoint: transport metadata and application mail input have different responsibilities. Persist the notification intent and its identity before attempting the send, then use the operation's documented idempotency convention when retrying.

For comparison, an Inngest-plus-Resend arrangement entails two service signups and two service credential sets. Application glue must carry the job identity into the email request and connect the send result to retry state. An existing cron system plus Resend can reuse that scheduler, but still needs the mail credential and the same identity handoff. Shared authentication reduces this credential boundary; it does not eliminate the adapter or the need for durable state.

A production adapter must use the documented request and response schemas rather than guess fields from endpoint names. The required acceptance test is concrete: consume a shipment job, derive exactly one notification intent, send it, then replay that same job and verify that the notification effect remains singular under the selected email delivery contract.

The following read-only preflight checks queue statistics before enabling a partner pipeline. Set BACKEND_BASE_URL to the configured service base ending in /v1, INFRAI_API_KEY to its secret credential, and QUEUE_NAME to an existing URL-safe queue name. It prints the response for inspection rather than inventing statistic field names. Curl retries transient responses, including HTTP 429, with exponential backoff and honors Retry-After; a terminal HTTP error remains visible and produces a failing exit status. No write is retried here.

This checks the queue, not duplicate safety.

If periodic scheduling initiates the workflow, use a cron trigger that enqueues work and let a worker process it. The managed cron execution limit is 900 seconds, and its target is a public HTTP URL rather than hosted application code. Paused schedules do not backfill missed triggers, trigger timing can jitter by seconds, and execution output retains only its first 4 KB. None of those properties supplies a durable notification ledger.

Start with one partner and a stated retry horizon. Establish receiver idempotency first, then move dispatch into the delayed queue. Test an acknowledgment lost after successful processing, a repeated job outside the five-minute deduplication window, and a recovery that approaches the application's record-expiration boundary. These are acceptance scenarios, not claimed test results.

Observe backlog and attempt rate together.

Keep aggregate metrics complete, sample diagnostic success traces where acceptable, and retain duplicate-protection records for the full recovery interval. Expand to another partner only after the queue drains under the permitted dispatch budget and replay cannot repeat a business effect.

The selection framework above distinguishes design requirements from product-specific settings. Consult these primary references for the latter before deploying.

#9731. How do you run AI agent evals in parallel on cloud GPUs?

Posted on Nov 7 • Originally published at nodus-compute.ai

Give every eval episode its own isolated sandbox, cap what each episode may spend, cap the whole batch, and let a separate grader score the answers. On Nodus that is one AgentGroup with a concurrency limit, a per-run model cap and a group cap, grading a fixed, versioned task set in sandboxes with no network. Parallelism shortens the wall clock but not the bill, since the same episodes use the same sandbox-minutes either way.

Most agent evals do not need a GPU at all. The agent thinks on a hosted model and runs commands and tests on a CPU. You need a GPU only when the task executes GPU code, or when you serve the model under test yourself.

A parallel eval needs four things: isolation per episode, a fixed task set, a grader the agent cannot reach, and limits that stop spend before it happens. Isolation keeps one episode's mistakes out of the next, and a separate grader keeps the agent away from the answer key.

Nodus covers each piece with a documented object. An Agent is a definition: a system prompt, the inference source and a cost cap. Each AgentRun is one conversation in its own sandbox.

An AgentGroup runs many runs of one agent at once, with maxActive between 1 and 1,000 (default 10) and one maxCostUSD for the group. An Environment is a versioned set of tasks with a grader, and the same name, version and seed always give the same tasks in the same order.

Grading is the part to get right. In a Nodus Environment, tasks carry a prompt and non-secret metadata only, and expected answers stay with the grader. Program graders run in grading sandboxes with no network access, and code from a completion runs as a separate user that cannot read the answers. Every verdict is Correct, Incorrect, InvalidOutput or InfrastructureFailure, and an infrastructure failure does not count toward the pass rate.

Define the agent with a per-run cap, then create an evaluation group that names an Environment at an explicit version. This is the example worker agent from the Agents guide, applied with nodus apply -f agent.yaml:

The evaluation itself, copied from the Evaluate an agent section of the same guide, runs two held-out tasks from a catalog Environment, two at a time:

Nodus generates the task batch, runs it through ordinary AgentRuns, and grades completed answers with the Environment's isolated grader. There is no submit or seal step. A batch holds at most 100 cases including repetitions, and every member pins the same Agent revision. Results record the Environment version, image digest, split and seed, so you can rerun the same eval later.

Agent evaluations are in Beta. Before you build on this example, confirm that your installed SDK version accepts evaluation= and group.results(). The console's Results view shows the same scored cases, pass rate and pending cases for each group. Plain parallel groups with submit_many and agent.map are documented on the Python Agents page if you grade answers yourself.

A failed run, missing answer or grader failure stays unscored instead of becoming a zero. That is the right call, and it is why pass rate should be read next to coverage, as we argue in Can an agent's pass rate rise while it completes fewer tasks?.

The per-run cap bounds one episode, and the group cap bounds the batch. perRunMaxCostUSD (default $1.00) is checked before every model call. When the next call would not fit, the run waits with MaxCostReached and makes no more calls. A runaway episode therefore stops at its cap instead of eating the batch.

The group cap is stricter than it looks. A run starts only when its own cap fits under what is left: the group cap, minus what the group has spent, minus the caps of runs still going. That gives a simple sizing rule we use: set the group cap to at least the number of tasks times the per-run cap, and every case is guaranteed room to start. Set it lower and you bound spend, but some cases may wait with MaxCostReached and end the batch unscored.

Both caps cover model usage only. The sandbox each run works in, and the grading sandboxes, are billed on their own. For one ceiling over compute and managed inference together, the Agents guide recommends a project-scoped Budget with period: Total and action: Block. This is the Budget example from the docs; change period to Total for an eval campaign:

With Block, new work in scope is refused with 402 BudgetExceeded and running work stops gracefully. We cover the same pattern for coding agents in How do you cap the GPU spending of an AI coding agent?.

Price the sandbox time and the model ceiling separately, because they behave differently. Take one full batch of 100 cases, each running about 10 minutes. That is 1,000 sandbox-minutes, or 16.67 sandbox-hours, whatever max_active you pick.

Prices checked November 7, 2026, on the Nodus pricing page; GPU rates are listed as hourly supply prices. The sum is 16.67 hours times the hourly rate, before any minimum charge per sandbox, which the Sandboxes dry-run estimate shows. New agent sandboxes start at one vCPU and 1 GiB under the Agents guide's Auto setting.

On a CPU sandbox the model is the bill; on an H100 the GPU is.

The model cap is a ceiling, not a forecast. Your real model spend is whatever the runs use, shown in status.cost. The lesson from the table is still clear: for a CPU-only agent eval, the sandbox is a rounding error and the model is the bill. Put an H100 under every episode and the GPU costs more than four times the model ceiling.

Parallelism moves the wall clock. With 100 ten-minute episodes, max_active of 1 takes 1,000 minutes, 10 takes 100 minutes, 25 takes 40, 50 takes 20, and 100 takes 10, ignoring startup and queueing. The sandbox-minutes stay at 1,000 in every case.

Same 1,000 sandbox-minutes in every bar; only the waiting changes.

Your model provider's rate limits can become the real ceiling on parallelism. If you bring your own key, Nodus charges nothing for the model, and your provider's rate and spending limits apply.

Use the cheapest place that can actually run the task. This is the decision rule we apply:

GPU sandboxes keep billing while idle, so give each one a short idleTimeout, a maxLifetime and its own maxCostUSD. The Sandboxes guide's quick start sets all three. From Python, nodus.Sandbox.create takes the same limits (Python Sandboxes). For the GPU sandbox options themselves, see Which sandboxes give AI agents GPUs?.

Size the batch by the error bar you can accept, then prefer new tasks over repeats. For a pass rate, the Central Limit Theorem standard error in Adding Error Bars to Evals (Miller, 2024) is the square root of p(1 - p) / n for binary scores. At a 50% pass rate over 100 independent tasks, the 95% interval is 1.96 x 0.05, or plus or minus 9.8 points. Quadrupling to 400 tasks halves it to plus or minus 4.9.

Repeats help less than new tasks. In the paper's worked example (binary scores, task difficulty uniform), K answers per task cut the variance to (1 + 2/K)/3 of a single answer. With one 100-case batch, that gives these trade-offs:

Spending cases on repeats instead of new tasks widens the error bar.

The arithmetic: 50 x 2 gives (1/50) x (2/3) = 1/75 against 1/100, a ratio of 1.33. 25 x 4 gives (1/25) x (1/2) = 1/50, a ratio of 2.00. The paper also warns that a pooled standard error across all repeated answers is inconsistent, so average each task's repeats first. Use repetitions when you have run out of distinct tasks, or when you want each task's own pass rate.

Two more points from the same paper are worth applying. When comparing two agents, analyze per-task paired differences rather than two headline numbers. And do not lower the sampling temperature just to make the score less noisy.

Keep the harness you have if it already works. The question is where it runs. Inspect AI runs samples in parallel and limits them with max_sandboxes, which for its Docker provider defaults to twice the processors available. The SWE-bench harness recommends at least 120 GB of free storage, 16 GB of RAM and 8 CPU cores, and fewer than min(0.75 * os.cpu_count(), 24) for --max_workers.

Those limits come from one machine. On a large workstation, a local Docker run is the simplest choice, and you should use it. Move to per-episode cloud sandboxes when one machine's cores cap your concurrency, or when you need hard spending caps and a grader isolated from the agent.

If you compare sandbox providers, read their billing rules. Modal, for example, bills Sandboxes at non-preemptible rates of 3x list price, $0.00003942 per physical core per second for CPU.

Not for the same episodes: each still gets one sandbox, the same minutes and the same model usage. What changes is how hard you push your model provider's rate limits.

It waits with MaxCostReached and makes no more model calls. The cap is copied when the run is created, so to continue you cancel it and start a new run with a higher cap.

Not in a Nodus Environment. Only task prompts reach the agent, and program graders run as a separate user in a sandbox without network access.

The timeout defaults to 30 minutes and can be set from 1 minute to 24 hours. It includes preparation, queueing and funding waits, and answers that could not be graded by then are reported as evaluation timeouts, outside the pass rate.

Report the pass rate with its standard error, plus how many cases were scored. A bare percentage hides both the noise and the missing cases.

#9730. CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

#9729. Software You Never Set Up Is Money You Wasted: How Firstep Configures the Dashboard for You

There is a particular kind of waste that almost every small business has paid for. An owner signs up for a promising piece of software, logs in, and finds a blank screen waiting to be configured. Fields to define, settings to choose, workflows to build. The owner, who has actual work to do, closes the tab and tells themselves they will set it up this weekend. They never do. The subscription renews anyway, month after month, for a tool that was never once used.

This is the hidden failure of most business software. The problem is rarely the features. It is the setup, the hours of configuration that stand between buying a tool and getting anything out of it, and that solo owners almost never have the time or patience to finish.

A customer relationship manager is the clearest example. Owners are told, correctly, that a CRM keeps a business organized by tracking customers and sales, sending reminders, handling quotes and invoices, and keeping every conversation in one place. All of that is true, and none of it matters if the system sits empty because no one built it out. An unconfigured CRM is just a more expensive spreadsheet that the owner is afraid to open.

The reason the blank dashboard usually wins is simple math. Setup is front-loaded work with a delayed payoff. The owner has to invest hours now, learning the software and entering the structure of their business, in exchange for benefits that only show up later. Faced with that trade-off against a day already full of paying work, most owners defer, and deferral quietly becomes never.

Firstep Business Solutions, a Dayton, Ohio company, takes the opposite approach by doing the configuration before the owner ever logs in. Its CRM arrives already built, with the company describing the result plainly: the business starts organized, professional, and easy to manage from day one. Rather than handing over an empty system, Firstep sets it up so the owner inherits a working dashboard instead of a project.

The part that makes this practical is the industry-specific automations. A generic CRM has to be told what a business does. Firstep’s comes pre-configured for the owner’s trade, with templates, workflows, and funnels relevant to that specific line of work already in place. A cleaning business and a catering business do not get the same blank canvas; they get dashboards shaped around how each actually operates. A landscaper might log in to find lead pipelines, booking workflows, and follow-up sequences already built for recurring seasonal service, rather than a set of empty fields asking what a pipeline should contain. That pre-configuration is the difference between a tool the owner has to translate into their business and one that already speaks their language.

“Small business owners shouldn’t have to become software experts just to run their business,” a Firstep spokesperson said. “We want to eliminate that learning curve by helping set up the tools and automations they need from the start. Instead of spending hours figuring out how to make everything work, they can focus on what matters most — growing their business.”

Setup sounds like a minor convenience. For a solo owner, it is actually the gatekeeper for everything else. A dashboard that is never configured is a dashboard whose payment tools, scheduling, follow-ups, and reminders all go unused too, because the owner never got far enough in to reach them. Solve the setup, and the rest of the platform becomes reachable. Leave it unsolved, and the most capable software in the world is just another renewing charge for a login no one visits.

Firstep bundles this done-for-you configuration into the same $97-per-month plan that handles formation and compliance, which reframes what the monthly fee buys. The money buys more than a set of tools. It buys tools someone has already made usable. The company says more than half of its orders since early 2024 have included ongoing services, which suggests owners stay when the software actually works in their day rather than waiting on a weekend of setup that never arrives.

The waste was never that small business owners bought bad software. It was that they bought good software and never crossed the gap between signing up and using it. Firstep’s wager is that the gap is the real product, and that an owner who logs in to a dashboard already built for their trade will use it, while an owner who logs in to a blank one will quietly pay for it and walk away.

This story was distributed as a release by Sanya Kapoor under HackerNoon’s Business Blogging Program

#9728. Rebuilding Praecepta: From a Trie to Bitsets, and a Fair Benchmark Against Camunda and Drools

Posted on Nov 7 • Originally published at bruno.pacheco.lu

In January 2023 I wrote about optimizing decision-making with a trie. The idea worked in principle: part of it was implemented, and is still maintained, at Pictet Tech. The numbers looked great, as you can see in my previous post.

Going through my old repositories for opportunities to test Claude, I decided to explore the major problem of that solution: the trie's memory exploded as tables grew; a generated table of 1,000 rules took over 1 GB. And during the development process, Claude told me that the first benchmark was not entirely fair, as Praecepta ran a different hit policy from Camunda and Kogito, and two of the services read one input from the wrong field.

So I refactored the engine and the benchmark, and completed the Maven plugin that compiles tables at build time. The result of the refactoring can be found in Praecepta 0.1.0 on Maven Central. The principles are still the same: a small, dependency-free Java engine for DMN decision tables. It now also has a website for the guide and the API documentation.

This post covers what changed, a benchmark against Camunda and Drools that I tried hard to make fair (including where it flatters Praecepta, and where Praecepta is slower), and what those engines do that Praecepta does not. This post also covers how open Praecepta is, and what could come next. That last part is where I would love your opinion.

A decision table is a simple list of rules. Each rule tests some input columns (country is "PT" or "ES", age in [18..65), or "anything") and produces outputs. The previous solution, a custom implementation of a trie, stored every possible path through the columns, and every "anything" cell multiplied the paths. That multiplication was the memory problem!

I tried a couple of things back then, including quantum computing via qengine: encoding the input as bits and each rule as quantum logic gates, to see whether a quantum circuit could beat the trie. It ran only on a simulator, but the thought stayed with me: rule matching is boolean logic over bits. The bitset index is the classical, practical version of that thought.

In the end, I stopped thinking about it. But now, in 2026, and with Claude's support, the new core uses bitsets. Every rule gets one bit. For every column, each distinct value the rules can tell apart gets a mask: the set of rules that accept it.

Rule 1 tests "PT", rule 2 tests "FR", rule 3 is "anything" (so it is in every mask), and rule 4 is not("FR"). Evaluating an input looks up one mask per column and ANDs them together. A 64-bit AND checks 64 rules at once, and the bundled 119-rule table fits in two words. Memory grows with columns × values × rules, never with the product of values, and the 1,000-rule table that needed 1 GB now takes 0.6 MB, and reading it from DMN and building it takes about a quarter of a second in a fresh JVM.

And the best part: the hit policy falls out of the bits too. Bits are numbered in rule order (or priority order), so FIRST is "lowest set bit", which is a single CPU instruction.

Numbers and dates work the same way: the boundaries the rules mention (18, 65, date("2025-01-01")) split each column into intervals, a binary search finds the interval, and each interval has its mask.

The core was not the only change. Praecepta now also has:

Since the first benchmark was not fair, I rebuilt it from scratch. This time Praecepta runs against Camunda 8 and Drools (the DMN engine inside Kogito), and every engine gets exactly the same work.

The bigger the table, the bigger the gap:

More columns cost Praecepta little: with 1,000 rules, going from 6 to 18 mixed columns takes it from 0.62 to 1.12 µs. Number and date columns cost it 2–3× string columns, because a binary search over decimals is slower than a hash lookup; that one has an issue.

Not every number is equally precise: 51 of the 63 latency measurements have a 99.9% confidence interval within ±10%. The widest is Drools on synthetic-10000, at ±33%. All of them are in the results, if you want to check.

Here, all three engines do well: they can be shared between threads, and all of them scale.

"First decision" starts a new JVM, reads the DMN file, builds the engine and evaluates one input. On the real table, Praecepta answers in 76 ms, 5–6× sooner than the others. That matters for command-line tools, serverless functions and test suites, and much less for long-running services.

"Retained heap" is the heap still in use after building the engine in a fresh JVM and running a garbage collection.

When it builds a FIRST or PRIORITY table, Praecepta looks for rules that can never fire: the validation described above. The check is exact, and on 1,000 random, overlapping rules it is expensive: 3.6 s under FIRST, and over a minute under PRIORITY. Evaluation is not affected, and the real 119-rule FIRST table builds in 74 ms. Still, a minute is not acceptable, and fixing it is on my list: issue #29 tracks making the check optional, bounded or cheaper.

Feeding a Map costs two hash lookups per column: one to read the value, one to find its mask. With the Maven plugin, inputs are generated records, and string columns with a value list become enums, whose masks are found by position instead of by hashing:

That is about 100 ns per decision on the real table, from an earlier run of the same code. But to keep the comparison fair, everything above uses Map inputs for every engine, Praecepta included.

Numbers like these are easy to oversell, so here is what they do not say.

Where the comparison flatters Praecepta, or is limited:

What Camunda and Drools do that Praecepta does not:

So, if your decisions are mostly decision tables with simple cell tests, and latency, memory or start-up matter to you, give Praecepta a try. If you need full DMN, Camunda and Drools are the better choice.

Using it is simple. First, add the engine (it has no dependencies):

Then load a DMN file, bind the inputs, and evaluate:

Or let the Maven plugin compile your tables (Excel, CSV or DMN) at build time:

The build fails if the table has errors (for example, two UNIQUE rules that overlap), and only the engine is needed at runtime. The README has the details.

I wanted a small project that is easy to trust. Here is what that means in practice:

The lowest Scorecard item is code review, and it is worth explaining. Anyone can fork the project and open a pull request. The check measures something else: whether each change that reached main was approved by someone other than its author. Today that is zero, because I am the only maintainer, and nobody can approve their own changes. The same reason keeps branch protection from a full score: I merge my own pull requests with an administrator's bypass. Every contribution I review raises the first, and a second maintainer would close both. The governance explains how to become one. Which brings me to the next part.

If you would like to contribute, the website gathers the guide, the API documentation and how the engine works, and the contributing guide explains how to build and test it. Here are some good first issues:

I would also welcome reviewers and a co-maintainer: the governance describes the roles and how decisions are made.

These are the features I think would be useful; the roadmap puts them in order for the next year. Tell me which ones you would use: a 👍 on the issue is enough, and a comment if you would like to build it.

The 2023 trie proved the idea and hit a wall. Bitsets took it further: on these tables, 20 to 2,000 times faster than general-purpose DMN engines, with 6 to 88 times less memory, and honest about what it does not do, including a build that is still slow for large FIRST and PRIORITY tables. Give it a try, tell me where it breaks, and tell me what you would like it to do next.

#9727. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

#9725. osFoundry처럼 Codex CLI를 Python으로 감싸는 방법

osFoundry 데스크톱 앱에서 Codex의 "로그인 확인"을 누르면 아래 명령이 실행된다. 명령을 조립하는 건 src-tauri/src/providers/agent_cli.rs의 build_codex_command이고, cli:codex:agent로 도는 실제 작업도 전부 이 함수를 거친다.

프로세스를 띄우기 전에 osFoundry는 자식 프로세스 환경에서 CODEX_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, OPENAI_BASE_URL을 뺀다. 이 값들이 남아 있으면 실행이 ChatGPT 로그인이 아니라 종량제 API 계정으로 과금되기 때문이다.

이 글에서 다루는 건 이 파이프의 반대편이다. 스트림 형식이 약속되지 않은 에이전트 CLI에서 답과 진행 상황, 그리고 깔끔한 실패를 꺼내야 한다.

지금 osFoundry는 2번이다. 파서는 runtime/session_event.rs의 parse_codex_line에 있고, 보는 게 생각보다 적다.

나머지 이벤트는 버리고, JSON이 아닌 줄도 건너뛴다. 스키마가 고정되지 않은 상대인데도 돌아가는 건 이 관대함 덕분이다. 모르는 이벤트 타입이 늘어도 손해가 없다. 깨질 수 있는 건 위 일곱 줄에 걸린 필드 이름이 바뀔 때뿐이다.

대신 단위가 굵다. Codex가 내보내는 건 토큰 델타가 아니라 완료된 아이템이다. 답은 메시지가 다 써진 순간에 한꺼번에 도착한다. 앱이 Codex에 "실시간 스트림 없음"을 붙이고 run-then-emit이라고 설명하는 이유다. 진행 줄은 아이템이 끝날 때마다 하나씩 온다.

이 Mac에는 Codex 바이너리가 없다. 그래서 fake_codex.py라는 대역을 만들었다. 같은 플래그를 받고, 위의 이벤트 타입을 정해진 지연으로 찍고, 종료할 때 -o 파일에 최종 메시지를 쓴다. 멈추기, 크래시, 인증 실패도 시킬 수 있다. Codex가 아니니까 잴 수 있는 건 래퍼 쪽 동작이지 Codex의 속도가 아니다.

대역의 타임라인은 이렇다. 0.4초에 reasoning이 나온다. 이어서 셸 자식 프로세스(sleep 0.8)를 띄운다. 그로부터 약 1.3초 뒤에 agent_message, 다시 0.2초 뒤에 turn.completed. 답 파일은 종료 시점에 쓴다.

래퍼 wrap.py는 Python 3.9.6 표준 라이브러리만 썼다. 이벤트 방식의 핵심만 추리면 이렇다.

파일 방식은 --json 대신 -o 로 띄우고, p.wait(timeout=…)로 기다린 다음, 파일이 있으면 읽는 게 끝이다.

환경은 Apple M1, macOS 15.8.1이다. 방식마다 20번 돌려 중앙값을 냈고, Popen 직전부터 time.monotonic()으로 쟀다(bench.py).

절대값은 대역의 sleep이 정한 숫자다. 대역과 상관없이 남는 건 두 가지다.

먼저 인증. 이벤트 방식은 로그인 문제라는 걸 구조화된 필드로 알려 준다. 파일 방식은 stderr 문장을 보고 짐작하는 수밖에 없다. osFoundry는 메시지를 짧은 단어 목록(401, unauthorized, please log in, sign in 등)과 대조해서 앱 쪽 로그인 안내를 띄운다.

다음은 메시지 뒤 kill. 여기서 두 방식의 답이 갈린다. 이벤트를 읽었다면 완전한 agent_message가 있고 turn.completed만 없다. 파일 방식은 아무것도 남지 않는다. osFoundry는 스트림 내용으로 판정한다. turn.failed/error가 왔거나 텍스트가 한 글자도 안 왔으면 실패고, 종료 코드는 판정에 넣지 않는다. turn.completed가 빠진 걸 "부분 결과"로 다루고 싶다면 손댈 곳이 바로 여기다.

osFoundry는 실행 전체를 tokio::time::timeout으로 감싼다. 자율 실행은 1,800초, 로그인 확인처럼 스트리밍하지 않는 완성은 300초다. 자식은 kill_on_drop(true)로 띄우기 때문에, 타임아웃으로 future가 버려지면 프로세스도 같이 죽는다.

그런데 에이전트 CLI는 자기 자식 프로세스를 따로 둔다. 대역은 "셸 도구"로 sleep 30을 띄우고 그걸 기다리며 멈춘다. 래퍼가 돌아오고 0.3초 뒤에 그 PID가 살아 있는지 확인했다.

걸린 시간은 같고 뒷정리만 다르다. 도구 자식이 stdout 파이프를 쥐고 있으면, EOF를 기다리는 식의 읽기에는 EOF가 끝까지 안 온다. 위 루프가 readline이 돌아오길 기다리지 않고 기한을 보는 이유다.

이런 CLI는 인증 오류와 panic을 stderr에 쓴다. osFoundry도 stderr를 파이프로 받아서 에러 메시지용으로 끝부분(에이전트 경로에서 약 4,000바이트)을 남긴다. 문제는 파이프 버퍼에 한계가 있다는 거다. 이 Mac에선 아무도 안 읽는 stderr에 정확히 65,536바이트를 쓴 시점에서 자식이 멈췄다(pipecap.py). 그래서 대역이 답하기 전에 약 200KB의 트레이스를 쓰게 해 봤다.

CLI는 아무도 안 읽는 쓰기에서 막히고, stdout은 안 닫히고, 실행은 기한 초과로 날아간다. 동시에 읽는 비용은 스레드 하나면 된다. 이거 모르고 붙이면 삽질 확정이다.

여기서 다룬 Codex 항목은 앱의 BYOK 키 다이얼로그 안 "외부 AI" 탭에 있다.

#9724. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our interactive demos, download our open-source models, and discover how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.
