#9709. ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation

💻 Code | 📊 Data | 🤖 Models | 📖 Documentation

Robots are learning to fold laundry, sort parts, and handle unfamiliar objects. But those demonstrations are often rather narrow and don't explain what a robot has learned or why it fails.

To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure.

Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control.

Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks: an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.

ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations, which are recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation, without requiring time-consuming teleoperation, in which a person remotely controls the robot. Researchers can easily vary these training experiences. For example, a team could generate more pushing or flipping demonstrations, then evaluate performance on tasks kept out of training.

Starting with ToyBlocks as our first FoundationWorld, we aim to extend the approach to increasingly complex environments.

Building on our earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2, MolmoBot, and MolmoSpaces, ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain.

As a FoundationWorld, ToyBlocks is designed around four requirements: (1) realistic physics and appearance, (2) automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale, (3) challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity, and (4) broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain.

Open-ended domains require modeling a wide range of objects and interactions, making it infeasible to fulfill all these requirements. ToyBlocks’ narrow scope, on the other hand, makes it possible to fulfill them all.

Within ToyBlocks' smaller setting, researchers can work toward investigating how a robot can learn to perform any reasonable task while being confident that the simulated arm and blocks behave very similarly to their physical counterparts.

A physical robot gripper above wooden blocks in the ToyBlocks setup.

ToyBlocks is not just about picking and stacking blocks: pictures and letters on the blocks' faces allow for searching, sorting, and arranging tasks. A robot may need to turn a block to see a hidden face before deciding where it belongs. Domain randomization – varying block size, table height, and other physical properties from scene to scene – tests how well models generalize as the geometry changes.

ToyBlocks automatically generates skills (behaviors for short tasks) and task demonstrations that can be used to train models or adapt previously trained models through additional training (fine-tuning). High-level reasoning models decide what to do; low-level action models control the robot’s movements. The framework can also be used to easily design experiments and validate hypotheses.

ToyBlocks uses reinforcement learning (RL) and motion planning, which computes how the robot should move, to generate skills for short-horizon tasks, which involve brief sequences of actions. Skill training takes place in Isaac Lab, Nvidia's open-source framework for robot learning in simulation. Through trial and error, these policies – models that choose the robot’s actions – learn non-prehensile skills such as pushing a block across the table or flipping it onto another face without picking it up. Skill generation can draw on privileged information – values the simulator can supply directly but a real robot cannot, such as a block's exact position and orientation – instead of estimating it from camera images. This enables the automatic generation of skills that would require teleoperation in the real world.

To generate demonstration data, a task-and-motion planner (TAMP) automatically selects and sequences the skills needed to solve a task and plans the robot’s movements between them. Running each plan in simulation produces a dataset of recorded demonstrations along with labels describing which task or skill the robot performs. ToyBlocks scales data generation through generating and executing hundreds of such plans in parallel on a single graphics processing unit (GPU), reaching up to 24 times real-time performance.

Acting from sensor observations adds a perception problem: a model has to estimate a block’s pose – its position and orientation – which the simulator could supply directly. To reflect real-world conditions, ToyBlocks trains models that map raw sensor observations to actions.

Execution of Molmo 2 (a high-level model) and ManiFlow (a low-level model) trained in ToyBlocks. Molmo 2 selects skills such as rotation and flipping, indicating the relevant block via a pointing interface, while ManiFlow controls the simulated arm to execute the commanded skills.

ToyBlocks' controllable data generator lets users create training mixtures that emphasize particular skills or fill gaps in existing datasets. Researchers can study how much data a model needs and which experiences help it generalize to unseen tasks. For example, they could test whether adding rotation and pick-and-place demonstrations improves flipping, or vary the balance of examples inside and outside a defined workspace region—evaluating their choices on tasks kept out of training. Importantly, evaluation of trained models generates metrics beyond success rates; it provides information such as execution speeds, forces exerted on objects, and task progress measured via the same specifications used by the planning module.

A webpage interface lets users connect Claude – or another frontier model – and use natural language to instruct the robot or try tasks, offering a way to explore how a model plans and acts without needing robotics expertise.

The evaluations below use ToyBlocks to study how training data and methods affect performance, spatial reasoning, generalization to new letters and block appearances, multi-step planning, transfer to physical robots, and frontier models that act through tools. Users can easily design their own tasks and measures to investigate other questions—for example, whether a model performs better when it selects objects by pointing or by issuing text commands such as "pick the yellow block."

Low-level action models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs), map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions.

The premise of VLAs is that, by pretraining on large-scale datasets, they can rapidly generalize to different scenarios or a specific workspace. However, evidence on how well these action models generalize remains conflicting. Some studies report that these action models are brittle to changes in inputs, such as different object layouts and lighting, whereas others show that VLAs generalize well. We argue that these studies often rely on real-world datasets with limited flexibility in spatial variations. ToyBlocks enables us to test how well action models generalize in a simple, easily reproducible setting with meaningful task-space diversity.

We design generalization tests that vary the skill sequences needed to complete an instruction, the letters or colors on the blocks, and the number of blocks in a scene. A stacking study can withhold four-block stacks from training, then test whether a model can combine familiar movements to build them. Workspace studies distinguish performance at new positions within a training region from performance beyond its boundaries, where the model has to extrapolate. We illustrate the study setup and findings below.

We consider four tasks: Stack, Unstack, Flip, and Rotate. For these tasks, we study interpolation (new configurations within the training range) and extrapolation (configurations beyond that range). For example, we evaluate generalization by training on scenarios where objects spawn only in the left region (green) and testing on the right region (orange), or by training on stack heights of 2 and 5 blocks and testing on heights 3 and 4.

Spatial generalization studies for VLA models (results based on ManiFlow, π0.5, and MolmoAct 2). Despite large-scale pretraining, these popular action models generalize poorly in the initial results. We improve generalization and analyze the contribution of each technique. The chart’s LoRA label stands for low-rank adaptation, a method for fine-tuning a model with a small set of trainable weight updates. We believe action model generalization remains far from solved; ToyBlocks provides a valuable testbed for systematically exploring generalization techniques.

Long-horizon tasks, which require many steps, allow us to measure how well models can plan a sequence of actions to solve them. Our framework enables us to create such long-horizon tasks, and create oracles – reference components that provide correct plans or actions – at both the high and low levels. This allows us to isolate whether the high-level planning or low-level execution failed when a model fails at a task. An example long-horizon task might be to spell “Ai2” with a block stack; because the letters may not be immediately visible, the agent must first choose actions that reveal information, and then plan and execute a sequence of actions to build the stack.

We evaluate hierarchical models with explicit high-level planning and low-level execution models. In this instance, we choose Molmo 2, a vision-language model (VLM), as the high-level planner, and ManiFlow as the low-level policy. Molmo 2 chooses the skill to execute and the block to execute it on, while the low-level model executes the instruction. We train low-level models such as ManiFlow to pause after completing the execution and query the high-level model for the next instruction. We evaluate the model’s planning abilities on three scenarios of increasing difficulty. The easiest scenario initializes with each character upright and facing the camera. The medium scenario has characters that may not be upright, and the hardest scenario contains characters that are not visible at the start of the episode.

Success rates on three-letter block-spelling tasks using Molmo 2 as the high-level reasoning model and either ManiFlow or a motion planner for low-level manipulation. An example task is “Stack Ai2”. Molmo 2 and ManiFlow are trained on ToyBlocks and evaluated across three difficulty settings and two generalization conditions.

Our experiments with agentic systems test how frontier models plan and act through tool calls. We study three settings using Claude Opus 5.5. In the search-and-spell setting, we expose ToyBlocks skills through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard for connecting AI applications to tools. The agent sees the scene through camera images, calls skills such as pick, flip, or rotate by pointing at a pixel, and decides when to search, build, or declare the task complete or impossible. The same MCP tools can execute either the scripted skills that generate ToyBlocks demonstrations (motion-planned pick and place, plus RL-based rotate and flip) or learned ManiFlow skills. ToyBlocks includes the framework behind these experiments, which also powers the natural-language web interface described earlier.

A frontier model (Claude Fable 5.1) controls a robot in a ToyBlocks world to search for and stack blocks into a tower spelling “Ai2.” During the episode, the agent muses, “I need to figure out whether pick-and-place naturally straightens orientation or if I need to correct it manually… I have 63 calls left, plenty to run a controlled test” (0:06). The agent later hypothesizes: “…maybe the gripper’s yaw is radial—pointing from the robot base toward the block” (0:15) and eventually confirms this hypothesis (0:26) before constructing the three-block tower, but the ‘A’ is sideways (1:11). Surprisingly, current frontier models often make similar perceptual errors (see the next figure), despite their impressive planning, spatial reasoning, and search capabilities.

For classical planning, the agent (our system using Claude Opus 5.5 to plan and choose actions) solves all 30 of a group of block-stacking tasks similar to ones that frontier models struggled with a few years ago, using text descriptions. It also solves 30 out of 30 while repeatedly observing camera images and choosing its next action in a closed loop.

In the search-and-spell setting, the agent had to generate stacks spelling out three-letter words. It had to find the blocks with the corresponding letters among up to eight blocks in the scene. Importantly, 50% of the scenes did not have blocks with all the required letters, rendering the task infeasible. In this case, we required the agent to state that the task is infeasible. We found that in this experiment, the agent was able to successfully solve or correctly declare infeasible 63% of the tasks. Errors were mostly caused by the agent confusing letters with look-alike letters (13%) or choosing an incorrect orientation for a letter in a stack (15%).

Our results also show that the agent was able to solve the task more efficiently when the blocks had semantic regularities, or patterns, taking advantage of such patterns to reason about occluded faces. For instance, in most of the infeasible scenes, when the blocks had no patterns, the agent correctly looked at all the blocks’ faces before declaring infeasibility, whereas it was able to declare infeasibility significantly faster when the blocks had semantic patterns.

Our third experimental setting asks whether an agent can learn how its skills behave, using experiments as a scientist would. When a skill behaves unexpectedly, the agent forms a hypothesis, designs a small test, and revises its understanding from the result. We expand on this idea by having an agent run its own experiments and write its own skill descriptions based on what it finds. These learned descriptions raise success rates from 24% with the default descriptions to 63%, outperforming the 36% achieved with descriptions written by a human expert.

Share of letter-block faces the agent had exposed by the end of each “search and spell” episode (bars averaged over 20 episodes; one marker per episode, styled by outcome). In a feasible task every letter of the three-letter target word is present; in an infeasible task, one letter is missing and the agent should say so. Each patterned block carries uppercase and lowercase instances of a letter, plus images that begin with the letter (e.g., A-block: apple, ant, A, 1, airplane, a); an unpatterned block’s six faces are randomized and unrelated. Correct: the tower spelled the word, or for infeasible tasks, the agent correctly declared the task impossible. Letter rotated or look-alike: the agent built the tower, but a letter was turned or a look-alike substituted, including five infeasible tasks declared solved with a look-alike in the missing letter’s place. Block fell out of reach; reported: a needed block was pushed out of the arm’s reach, so the agent reported that its task had become impossible. No report: the agent used up its motor-skill budget and stopped without claiming either outcome. With patterned blocks, the agent finishes having seen fewer faces, because it can infer what hidden faces must depict rather than checking every one.

Action-conditioned world models are trained to predict how a scene changes in response to a robot’s actions. Using them as an alternative to model-based simulators for training and evaluating robot policies is an active area of research. How well they serve this purpose depends on how accurately they predict physical interactions, which is hard to measure without knowing the true state of the scene. ToyBlocks provides this ground truth – the actual simulated scene state – enabling highly controlled tests of how recently developed world models perform in low-level object manipulation. Here, the arm’s end effector is its gripper.

Specifically, we tested whether action-conditioned world models are capable of predicting the motions of blocks or the outcomes of skill executions after being trained on example executions. To do so, we chose four different skills (pick-and-place, flip, rotate, and a mixed task) and generated 900 trajectories – sequences of robot states and actions over time – for each skill. 50% of these trajectories were successful demonstrations of the skill, and 50% were unsuccessful because of small changes to spatial configurations. With equal numbers of successful and unsuccessful executions, a model that always predicts success would be correct only half the time. The models were fine-tuned on these demonstrations and then tested on their ability to predict the outcome of action sequences of the same skills.

We find that Wan 2.2 predicts block motion and task outcomes most accurately. Astra tracks the gripper well but struggles to simulate contact. LeWM is fast and more accurate over short interaction segments, though it drifts over full trajectories. In additional experiments, we also showed that models that score higher on pose and success prediction also produce better training data: adding 100 model-generated trajectories (rollouts) from the best video-generation model raises a policy’s success in an unseen region from 19% to 78%.

We tested three types of models: a video prediction model with 5 billion parameters (Wan 2.2), an agentic model that created its own physics simulator tuned to match the demonstration data (Astra), and a latent world model (LeWM). During testing, each trained model has to predict future images, simulator states, or latent states (learned internal representations), respectively, based on an initial image and a sequence of actions. For full trajectories, models use the initial image as the only observed image, along with the action sequence. For short interaction segments – a single pick, place, flip, or rotate – models start from the real image immediately before that interaction. Full trajectories show how errors accumulate over long horizons, while interaction segments isolate a single interaction, such as the gripper making contact with a block, and show how well the model predicts it. To compare models fairly, we probe each model’s predictions, reading out where it expects the blocks and gripper to be at different points in the trajectory and whether it expects the task to succeed at the end.

Sim-to-real evaluations test policies trained in simulation on physical robots performing block manipulation tasks. By comparing simulation and real-world execution, we assess whether behaviors and failure patterns observed in simulation provide meaningful indications of real-world performance. For example, researchers can evaluate individual skills and their composition in longer-horizon tasks to identify where failures arise and whether these patterns carry over to physical deployments.

We test whether the models trained entirely on ToyBlocks simulation datasets can be deployed in the real world zero-shot, without training on real-world examples. We evaluate ManiFlow and each low-level skill (pick, place, flip, and rotate) individually. We test whether the hierarchical system (Molmo 2 + ManiFlow) can complete long-horizon three-block spelling tasks requiring sequences of these actions. Real-world experiments use a Franka FR3 arm with a Robotiq gripper across thirty scene configurations. Each scene contains 4–10 blocks seen during training. An episode is successful only if the relevant blocks are moved to target poses without collisions. If the operator intervenes to stop the robot due to an unsafe motion during an episode, it is marked as a failure.

ManiFlow’s atomic-skill success rates were similar in simulation and the real world (80.0% and 81.1%). The hierarchical Molmo 2 + ManiFlow system succeeded in 55.5% of simulated episodes (111/200) and 50.0% of real-world episodes (15/30); further trials are needed to establish statistical confidence across tasks.

Success rates of the ManiFlow low-level model and the hierarchical Molmo 2–ManiFlow system in simulation and the real world. For ManiFlow, the total count represents individual skill executions (pick, place, flip, and rotate), whereas for Molmo 2–ManiFlow, it represents block-spelling task episodes. The Molmo 2–ManiFlow evaluations use the easiest scene configuration defined in the simulation evaluation, with block characters visible and upright.

Side-by-side real-world and simulated block-stacking executions using the same high-level planner. Pink rings mark the planner’s target point for each skill. The scenes use different block labels, and simulation playback is retimed to align grasps and releases with the real robot.

To transfer Molmo 2 and ManiFlow – both trained exclusively on ToyBlocks data – to a physical robot, we address the differences between simulation and reality in three stages.

Before data generation, we perform system identification by tuning simulated robot parameters, including joint friction and armature (the motor and gearbox inertia reflected at the joint), to match real-robot trajectories. During data generation, we randomize physical properties (object size, friction, and table height) and visual properties (lighting, backgrounds, materials, and camera parameters). At inference time, observations are captured using a front-facing ZED camera and a wrist-mounted ZED Mini. For policies that use depth images, we generate clean depth maps, which estimate distance at each pixel, from paired red-green-blue (RGB) camera images using FastFoundationStereo, rather than relying on noisy depth sensor measurements.

The physical ToyBlocks setup: a robot arm, wooden blocks, and a camera.

ToyBlocks connects data generation, training, and evaluation in one controlled setting, so researchers can investigate how robots learn over time and test how changes to a model or its training data affect robot behavior. We’re releasing simulation assets, procedural task and demonstration generators, automatically generated demonstrations, two trained models showcasing what the framework can do (one based on Molmo 2 and one based on ManiFlow), training code, and evaluation code and validation sets. This allows other teams to build their own training mixtures and investigate failure modes beyond those covered in our initial experiments.

Our initial data release is a proof point with 85,336 long-horizon demonstrations, each comprising about 6–12 skill demonstrations, depending on the set. The initial datasets cover nearly 1,600 hours of robot execution data and 144 million frames. In a few weeks, we're targeting a second release with a larger-scale dataset, more skills, and more comprehensive benchmarking. We’ll also add fully integrated RL training capability that is not contained in the current package.

Other directions for ToyBlocks include bimanual (two-arm) manipulation and dexterous robot hands, equipped with force and touch sensors for studying motion and tasks that involve frequent physical contact. We're also exploring play with unstructured piles of blocks as a way to collect data and study how new behaviors and tasks might emerge through interaction.

Future direction: RL-based pile manipulation.

Future direction: bimanual block manipulation.

With ToyBlocks, we want to advance the science of robot learning toward a future where robots can reliably apply what they've learned to unfamiliar tasks and environments. We encourage the research community to explore ToyBlocks for their own investigations and even as a basis to build their own FoundationWorlds.

#9708. How to keep the same character across AI video clips with reference images (Kling 3.0 Omni, MiniMax H3, Wan, Seedance)

Posted on Nov 7 • Edited on Nov 7 • Fully Autonomous

The most common complaint about AI video is not quality. It is that clip two shows a different person from clip one. You describe "a woman with a copper-red bob and an olive jacket", and the model draws a new woman who fits that description every time you press Generate.

The fix that works is reference images: you show the model the same few photos of your character on every clip, and you stop describing her in words. This tutorial walks through how to do that, which photos to pick, how to write the prompt, and how the main reference models differ: Kling 3.0 Omni, MiniMax H3 (Hailuo), Wan 3.0 and Seedance 2.5. Every image below is a frame from a real, unedited clip we made in RefVid, the tool I work on.

Our test character is Mia. She is invented, not a real person, which matters later (some models refuse real-looking faces, and you should only ever use photos of people who agreed to it).

She has four reference images, and the set is the whole trick:

Reference 1 of 4: the front view. The sharpest, most evenly lit photo goes first.

Reference 3 of 4: the profile. Without it, a model has to guess her nose and ear when she turns.

Rules that held up across every model we tried:

Once the photos are attached, the prompt should only say where she is, what she does and what the camera does. Do not repeat her hair colour or her jacket. When the words and the photos disagree even slightly, the model blends them, and the blend is the drift you were trying to avoid.

Here is the prompt for the first clip, word for word:

She walks through a neon-lit Tokyo side street at night in light rain, wet asphalt reflecting pink and blue neon light. The camera tracks alongside her at shoulder height in a smooth lateral dolly as she walks.

Kling 3.0 Omni, 5 seconds, from the four photos. Not edited.

Then the same four photos with completely different scenes:

Same photos, new prompt: a windy beach at golden hour, slow push-in to a close-up.

Same photos: a Scandinavian kitchen in morning light, pouring coffee, then smiling at the camera.

Same photos: a misty pine trail, turning back toward the camera.

Four scenes, four lighting setups, one face. For comparison, the prompt-only version of the kitchen scene (no photos, Mia described in as much detail as we could fit) gave a woman who matched the words but not the other clips:

Words only, no reference images. Close, but not Mia.

All of the Mia clips above ran on Kling 3.0 Omni, which takes up to 10 reference images and makes 3 to 15 seconds. If you want to try it without the Kling app or an API key, our Kling 3.0 Omni free online page runs a first 5-second clip on it for free.

Reference images are not a Kling feature; most current video models have a reference mode. The useful part is that the same saved photos work on all of them, so you can pick a model per shot and the character stays put. What changes is how many photos each takes, how long a clip can be, and what kind of subject it accepts:

A new account's free credits cover one short first clip from your photos on several of these: MiniMax H3 (5 seconds at 768p, with sound), Wan 3.0 (4 seconds at 720p) and Vidu Q4, another reference model that takes 1 to 10 photos.

Hailuo's original subject reference model, S2V-01, read a single face photo. MiniMax H3 reads several. We sent it the same four Mia photos:

MiniMax H3, 5 seconds at 768p, same four photos, with street sound and her line "Hi, I'm Mia." Back in 33 seconds.

The differences between S2V-01 and H3 are laid out in our Hailuo subject reference guide.

Most Wan reference-to-video tutorials are ComfyUI workflows written for Wan 2.6 or 2.7. Wan 3.0 takes up to 10 reference images and runs up to 30 seconds in one pass, which is the easiest way to keep a character through a long continuous action instead of stitching 5-second clips. Write the actions in order, one per sentence, so the model knows the sequence. More in Wan reference to video online.

Seedance 2.5 refuses photos of real-looking people before the clip runs. For a product, a pet or an illustrated character it holds detail very well. Here is AERO 1, an invented running shoe, from three product photos:

Seedance 2.5, 5 seconds at 720p, from three photos. The knit upper, heel tab and white sole match the photos.

For an illustrated character, a reference sheet that shows it from several sides works as one of the photos. Details in Seedance reference to video.

If you try this and a model still drifts on your character, tell me in the comments which model and how many photos you used. That is usually where the answer is.

#9706. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features

Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.

To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.

When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows).

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab.

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts.

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. #9705. The best apples for apple pie: Here's how to choose.: We put six varieties to the test.

Which are the best pie apples? With apple-picking season hard upon us, it's time to dust off your favorite apple pie recipe, sharpen your crust-rolling skills, and get ready to enjoy fall's favorite dessert: apple pie.

You may be tempted to make your pie from one of the six apple varieties that dominate the domestic market year-round: Red Delicious, Golden Delicious, Gala, Fuji, Granny Smith, and McIntosh.

But when fall rolls around, farmers' markets and orchard farm stands offer an abundance of apple choices.

You've probably identified your favorite eating apple. But what about the best pie apples? They're not necessarily the same. Red and Golden Delicious, for instance, are reliably crisp, sweet-eating apples. But when you bake them into a pie, they can become mushy and lose some of their sweetness. So what are the best apples for pie?

We'll put six different pie apples to the test.

The pie apples: I decide to put two of my favorites, Golden Russet and Northern Spy, up against a couple of classic pie apples: McIntosh and Cortland. I also add Granny Smith because, if there's one ubiquitous, year-round apple, Granny Smith is it. Ginger Gold — a Golden Delicious cross with Albemarle Pippin — is another variety that's often available in fall, and a worthy representative of the Delicious family.

And yes, there are plenty of other apple varieties to choose from: Fuji, Gala, Honey Crisp, and so many more. But with limited time and resources — and a pan with space for just six pies — I'm not able to test every apple out there. But if you want to choose the best pie apples among your personal favorites, you can have fun doing this same test at home.

I use a muffin tin to bake apples sweetened with a bit of sugar. To mimic apple pie (sans crust), I pile sliced apples high in the pan. Then I bake them in a preheated 425°F oven for 20 minutes, lower the oven temperature to 375°F, and continue to bake the apples until they're bubbly, about 40 minutes.

I had no idea there'd be such significant differences in both texture and flavor. For example, Russets and Macs are sweetened with the same amount of sugar, bake at the same temperature, for the same amount of time —  and offer way different results.

So, Granny Smith looks like the best combination of both taste and texture. Does it make the very best apple pie?

Not necessarily. I've baked many pies with this all-purpose apple, especially during the winter when other apples are scarce or pricey. A pie made 100% with Granny Smith apples is a mighty fine pie. But in fall, when every apple variety in the world is seemingly at your fingertips, why not take advantage of one or two (or more) of your own local favorites?

At the end of the day, choosing the best pie apples is a personal decision. My best apple pie would include a combination of these three: Cortland, for flavor; Russet, for texture; and Granny Smith, for its combination of the two.

What apples would fill your best pie? Bake your favorite varieties side by side and see what happens; the results may surprise you.

Please share your favorite apples for pie — and your favorite apple pie tips! — in comments, below.

#9704. Schlägt semantische Code-Suche grep wirklich in einem echten Repository?

Der Pitch fürs Einbetten einer Codebasis ist immer dieselbe Demo: Man fragt „Wo sperren wir Nutzer aus?“, grep findet nichts, weil der Code das Cooldown nennt, und die Vektorsuche landet in der richtigen Funktion. Eine gute Demo. Die Frage ist, wie oft das bei Code funktioniert, den niemand für die Demo ausgesucht hat.

Hier also eine Messung an einem Repository, das die meisten Python-Entwickler irgendwann gelesen haben: psf/requests im Tag v2.32.3, mit zehn Fragen, bei denen grep nach der naheliegenden Formulierung null Zeilen liefert. Die Pipeline kopiert die, die die osFoundry-Desktop-App für ihren Index lokaler Ordner benutzt (Chunking-Regeln aus folder_index.rs, hybrides Ranking aus folder_search.rs), in unter 200 Zeilen Python nachgebaut und auf einem Mac M1 mit 8 GB ausgeführt, nur CPU. Die kurze Antwort: Embeddings allein fanden den richtigen Chunk bei 4 von 10 Fragen unter den Top 5. Ein schlichtes Keyword-Ranking derselben Frage fand 6. Beide zusammen fanden 7 in den Top 10, und 9, sobald Tests und Doku nicht mehr mit dem Quellcode konkurrierten.

Embeddings arbeiten mit Stücken, nicht mit Dateien. Die App schneidet jede Datei in Chunks von etwa 700 Tokens mit 80 Tokens Überlappung, wobei ein Token als 4 Zeichen angenähert wird, und behält die erste und letzte Zeile jedes Chunks, damit ein Treffer als path:start-end gemeldet werden kann.

Chunks werden an Zeilengrenzen geschnitten, nie mitten in einer Zeile, und die letzte Absicherung ist wichtig: Eine minifizierte Datei mit einer einzigen 200-KB-Zeile würde sonst endlos zum selben Start zurückspringen.

Der Scan davor überspringt node_modules, dist, build, .git, .venv und ähnliche Ordner, Lockfiles anhand des vollen Namens (package-lock.json und pnpm-lock.yaml enden nicht auf .lock, weshalb ein reiner Endungsfilter sie übersieht), Dateien über 1 MB und alles mit einem Nullbyte in den ersten 512 Bytes. Bei requests blieben davon 117 von 129 Dateien übrig (10 binär, 1 über 1 MB, 1 ausgeschlossenes SVG), 625.261 Bytes und 318 Chunks.

Eines verbirgt die 4-Zeichen-Regel: Code lässt sich schlechter tokenisieren als Fließtext. Mit dem eigenen Tokenizer von bge-m3 gemessen lag der mittlere Chunk bei 771 Tokens, nicht bei 700, der längste bei 2.050. Das spielt im nächsten Schritt eine Rolle.

Die Skripte laufen mit uv run, das sentence-transformers und torch aus den Inline-Metadaten am Anfang jeder Datei installiert. Zum Vergleich liefen dieselben Chunks auch durch bge-small-en-v1.5, ein englisches Modell mit 33 Mio. Parametern, etwa 17-mal kleiner (seine Anfragen bekommen das vom Modell empfohlene Präfix „Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: “).

Zehn Minuten für ein Repository mit 625 KB sind langsam, etwa 2 Sekunden pro Chunk auf diesem Rechner, und der Aufwand wächst mit dem Code, nicht mit der Dateizahl. Er fällt nur einmal an: Die App schlüsselt Chunks nach einem Hash ihres Textes, ein unveränderter Chunk behält also seinen Vektor, und das Ändern einer Funktion bettet nur eine Handvoll Chunks neu ein. Die Geschwindigkeit des kleinen Modells hat einen Haken, den die Tabelle deutlich zeigt: Bei 512 Tokens las es von 235 der 318 Chunks nur den Anfang.

Eine Regel markiert der Quelltext der App mit einer roten Markierung, und sie lässt sich im eigenen Code leicht brechen. Die Anfrage muss mit demselben Modell eingebettet werden, das den Index gebaut hat. Ein bge-m3-Chunk-Vektor und ein Anfragevektor eines anderen Modells mit 1.024 Dimensionen haben dieselbe Form, also gibt es keinen Fehler, und die Ergebnisse sind einfach falsch.

grep bekam die Formulierung, die man eintippen würde, ohne Beachtung der Groß-/Kleinschreibung, über dieselben 117 Dateien. Als fairere Keyword-Baseline lief die ganze Frage außerdem durch BM25 über die Chunks, wobei Bezeichner an _ und camelCase getrennt wurden, damit should_strip_auth auf „strip“ passt. (Die Keyword-Seite der App ist tantivy über ganze Dateien, abgebildet auf die ersten Chunks jeder Datei; das Ranking pro Chunk ist eine Vereinfachung.)

Die beiden Rankings werden mit Reciprocal Rank Fusion bei k = 60 verschmolzen, derselben Konstante wie in der App, mit den Top 30 jeder Liste:

RRF ignoriert die Scores und nutzt nur die Positionen, und genau das ist der Punkt. Ein BM25-Score und eine Kosinus-Ähnlichkeit liegen nicht auf derselben Skala, und den einen gegen den anderen zu normalisieren erfindet einen Zusammenhang, den es nicht gibt. Ein Chunk, der in einer Liste auf Platz 3 und in der anderen auf Platz 5 steht, schlägt einen, der in einer Liste auf Platz 1 steht und in der anderen fehlt.

Die Antwort für jede Frage ist der Chunk mit der def-Zeile der Zielfunktion, ausgewählt durch Lesen des Codes, bevor irgendetwas lief. Angegeben ist der Rang dieses Chunks unter allen 318.

Die Ränge beziehen sich auf 318 Chunks; die grep-Zahlen sind passende Zeilen. „Hybrid“ ist BM25 verschmolzen mit bge-m3.

Dass grep bei einer Formulierung null liefert, heißt nicht, dass Keywords nutzlos sind. Über die Wörter der Frage gerankt, setzte BM25 die Antwort bei 6 der 10 in die Top 5. „Redirect“, „proxy“, „401“ und „UTF-16“ kommen alle im Code vor; nur die Formulierung drumherum passt nicht. Die Ein-Wort-Suchen zeigen das umgekehrte Problem: 625 Zeilen für GET, 98 für bytes. Sie finden die Stelle irgendwo in einem Haufen, den man dann von Hand liest.

Die Erfolge der Embeddings sind echt, aber speziell. bge-m3 fand should_strip_auth auf Platz 1 bei einer Frage, die kein Wort mit der Funktion teilt, und holte rebuild_method von Platz 65 bei BM25 auf Platz 10. Das kleine Modell setzte atomic_open bei „never left half-written if the process dies“ auf Platz 1, wo BM25 es auf 58 hatte; der Docstring dieser Funktion sagt „atomic fashion“, und das Modell weiß, was atomar bei einer Datei bedeutet. Und Vektoren scheitern auf Arten, die Keywords nicht kennen. Beim reinen Bezeichner raise_for_status setzte bge-m3 den definierenden Chunk auf Platz 70, bge-small auf 244.

Die Verschmelzung ist der sicherere Standard, nicht in jeder Zeile der beste. Bis auf die eine Frage, die keiner fand, war Hybrid nie die schlechteste Spalte und meist nah an der besten, und genau das will man von einem Werkzeug, das man aufruft, ohne vorher zu wissen, welche Art von Frage man hat. „How big is the body“ scheiterte überall: super_len sagt nie in Worten, die eine Frage benutzen würde, was es misst.

Die meisten Fehlgriffe waren nicht zufällig. Bei „why does a POST turn into a GET“ war das erste Ergebnis von bge-m3 tests/test_requests.py, rund um test_http_303_changes_post_to_get. Bei „read saved logins from a file in the home folder“ war es der Changelog-Eintrag zu .netrc in HISTORY.md, und bei „move the upload back to the start“ und „how big is the body“ ein Abschnitt in docs/user/advanced.rst. Tests und Doku beschreiben Verhalten in einfachen Worten, genau wie eine Frage, und liegen ihr deshalb oft näher als die Implementierung.

Das ist keine falsche Antwort, denn der Test nennt die Funktion. Aber das Ranking ändert sich stark, sobald man sie herausfiltert. Bei einer Suche nur in den 84 Chunks unter src/ mit denselben Vektoren fand die Hybridsuche 9 von 10 in den Top 10. Die billigste Verbesserung in diesem Repo war kein größeres Modell, sondern ein Pfadfilter, oder wenigstens eine Kennzeichnung von Test- und Doku-Treffern, damit man sie überspringen kann.

Das kleinere Modell hielt mit, obwohl es bei den meisten Chunks nur die ersten 512 Tokens las, wahrscheinlich weil die ersten Zeilen eines Chunks, mit dem def und seinem Docstring, das meiste davon tragen, worum es geht. Zehn Fragen an einem Repository reichen nicht, um eines der beiden Modelle besser zu nennen. Sie reichen, um zu sehen, dass die Modellwahl weniger zählte als die Verschmelzung mit Keywords und das Fernhalten der Tests.

Beim ersten Lauf von embed.py wird bge-m3 von Hugging Face geladen, etwa 2,3 GB. Die Anfragen sollten vor dem Blick auf die Ergebnisse geschrieben und die Antworten durch vorheriges Lesen des Codes festgelegt werden. Es ist sehr leicht, die Formulierung einer Frage so lange anzupassen, bis die Vektorsuche gewinnt.

Die Desktop-App osFoundry führt dieselbe Pipeline über ihren Indexes-Bildschirm aus, mit bge-m3 auf dem Gerät und BM25 und Vektoren verschmolzen in ihrem Agent-Tool folder_search. Der Chunking-Eintrag im Glossar behandelt die Abwägungen bei Chunk-Größe und Überlappung, und die App ist auf der osFoundry-Download-Seite kostenlos erhältlich.

#9701. Bagaimana osFoundry mencegah edit dari Claude menimpa edit seseorang di Note yang sama?

Inilah tool tulis yang didapat chat Claude untuk Notes di osFoundry, sesuai daftar di endpoint MCP publiknya. Data ini diambil lewat tools/list tanpa autentikasi pada 2026-11-06, lalu dipangkas ke field yang relevan di sini:

Dua dari lima field wajib sama sekali tidak berhubungan dengan isi edit. expected_version membuat penulisan menjadi compare-and-swap: write hanya masuk kalau Note masih berada di versi yang dibaca agent. idempotency_key membuat pengiriman ulang tidak berbahaya. Write Note lainnya, create_note_tab dan add_note_source, juga mewajibkan pasangan yang sama. Read tidak: list_note_tabs, read_note_tab, read_sheet_range (paling banyak 100 kali 100 sel) dan list_note_attachments semuanya readOnlyHint: true di bawah osfoundry:read.

Di bawah ini apa yang didapat dari kontrak itu, diukur pada sebuah rebuild. Pengecekan versi baru separuhnya. Separuh lainnya adalah apa yang dilakukan agent setelah write-nya ditolak.

replace_text mengirim seluruh teks sebuah tab. Kalau Claude membaca versi 7, seseorang menyimpan versi 8, lalu Claude mengirim teksnya, server memegang dua dokumen utuh dan satu ancestor bersama yang sudah tidak ia simpan lagi. Server tidak bisa tahu apakah Claude memang ingin menghapus paragraf baru orang itu atau memang tidak pernah melihatnya. Last-writer-wins memilih jawaban yang salah tanpa suara. Menolak adalah satu-satunya respons yang tidak menebak.

Itulah optimistic concurrency. Tidak ada yang memegang lock selama model berpikir dua puluh detik. Setiap write menyebutkan versi yang menjadi dasarnya, dan server hanya melakukan swap kalau versi itu masih yang terbaru:

Aplikasi desktop osFoundry melakukan hal yang sama dari sisi manusia. Di apps/web/src/screens/notes/context/NotesContext.tsx, penyimpanan Note adalah PATCH /notes/:id yang membawa expected_updated_at (revisi server terakhir yang dilihat editor) dan, setelah write dari Connected, sebuah expected_version yang disimpan connected-note-save-guard.ts di localStorage supaya tidak hilang saat reload. Kalau penyimpanan gagal, editor menyimpan konten orang itu sebagai draft lokal dan menampilkan error sinkronisasi. Kedua editor sama-sama melakukan conditional write.

Ada dua reaksi yang masuk akal, dan hanya satu yang benar-benar bekerja:

Cara kedua lolos pengecekan tapi tetap menimpa edit orang itu, karena payload-nya dihitung dari teks lama. Pengecekan tidak bisa melihat hal itu. Versi hanya membuktikan bahwa kamu sudah melihat nomor versi terbaru, bukan bahwa kamu memakai isinya.

Tidak ada binary Claude yang berjalan di sini. notes_store.py mengimplementasikan list_note_tabs, read_note_tab, read_sheet_range, edit_note_tab (replace_text, sheet_set_range) dan create_note_tab di atas sqlite dalam mode WAL, dengan nama tool dan nama argumen yang sama seperti versi live. Setiap write berjalan di dalam BEGIN IMMEDIATE: cek tabel idempotency, bandingkan versi, terapkan, naikkan versi, dan simpan hasilnya, semuanya dalam satu transaksi. race.py menjalankan dua thread dengan koneksi masing-masing: "Claude" yang di-script dan seseorang yang di-script. Masing-masing melakukan read → think → write, 100 kali. Waktu berpikir diperkecil: 20–80 ms untuk Claude, 5–40 ms untuk orang itu, sehingga jendela read-ke-write milik agent lebih panjang, seperti pada model sungguhan. Setiap write menambahkan satu baris unik (claude-17, human-42), jadi setelahnya baris yang hilang adalah lost update yang bisa dihitung. Python 3.9.6, Apple M1, seed 1–5.

Dan loop agent-nya, dengan saklar policy:

Percobaan yang kena conflict mendapat idempotency key baru. Key itu menamai satu write yang dimaksud di atas satu base. Setelah ditolak, write yang diterapkan ulang adalah write yang berbeda.

Lima run, 100 edit per editor per run, total 1,000 baris yang dimaksud per baris tabel:

Tanpa pengecekan, 30% dari semua edit lenyap, dan orang itu kehilangan lebih banyak daripada Claude. Waktu berpikir agent yang lebih panjang membuat write-nya didasarkan pada read yang lebih lama, jadi lebih banyak menimpa. Dengan pengecekan dan penerapan ulang, tidak ada yang hilang. 41–48% write Claude butuh percobaan kedua, tidak pernah yang ketiga. Rata-ratanya 1.41–1.48 percobaan untuk Claude dan 1.24–1.30 untuk orang itu. Setiap run memakan 9.6–10.5 s wall time apa pun mode-nya, karena waktu berpikir yang dominan.

Baris ketiga adalah yang perlu diingat. Server melaporkan lebih dari 300 conflict dan tidak melindungi apa pun. Pengecekan versi memaksa kamu membaca ulang. Ia tidak bisa memaksa kamu memakai apa yang kamu baca.

bench.py mengukur waktu 2,000 panggilan edit_note_tab berurutan dengan replace_text 200 karakter, tiga kali pengulangan per mode. Median per write: 61.9–63.1 µs tanpa pengecekan, 57.0–58.8 µs dengan versi Note, 55.1–61.1 µs dengan versi tab. Perbandingannya hanya satu read ber-index di dalam transaksi yang memang sudah terbuka. Selisihnya di bawah noise antar-run. p99 (0.42–1.33 ms) adalah jitter fsync sqlite dan tidak mengikuti mode.

Deskripsi tool osFoundry mengikat satu versi ke seluruh Note. create_note_tab menyebut "Use the version from list_note_tabs", yaitu listing di level Note. Di jalur apply aplikasi desktop untuk edit Connected (connected-note-application.ts), expected_version dibandingkan dengan updated_at milik Note. Jadi seseorang yang mengetik di tab Sheet menggeser versi yang dipakai untuk mengecek write Claude ke tab teks.

Di rebuild, hal ini bisa diukur. Jalankan race.py tabs dengan Claude mengedit tab teks dan orang itu menulis sel di tab Sheet, 3 run, masing-masing 100 edit:

Ke-217 conflict itu semuanya palsu, karena kedua editor tidak pernah menyentuh tab yang sama. Biayanya masing-masing hanya satu read ulang, tidak lebih. Versi level Note memberi sesuatu yang tidak bisa diberikan versi tab: setiap write dicek terhadap seluruh isi Note, jadi agent yang membaca Sheet untuk menulis Brief tidak bisa menulis Brief berdasarkan nilai Sheet yang sudah berubah di tengah jalan. Versi level tab menghilangkan conflict palsu, tapi justru kehilangan jaminan lintas-tab itu. Untuk agent yang membaca satu tab dan menulis ke tab lain, versi yang kasar ini adalah default yang lebih aman.

Versi berbasis timestamp hanya bekerja kalau dua penyimpanan tidak mungkin menghasilkan string yang sama. race.py fast menurunkan waktu berpikir ke nol, 2,000 edit per editor, 5 run, lalu membandingkan versi yang dipotong ke milidetik dengan timestamp mikrodetik plus suffix 6 digit hex:

Kalau dua write di-commit di milidetik yang sama, write kedua mendapat versi yang sama dengan yang pertama. Editor yang membaca sebelum write pertama lalu lolos pengecekan terhadap write kedua. osFoundry menyimpan versi Note dengan presisi timestamp PostgreSQL penuh. Kalau kamu membangun sendiri, pakai counter, atau timestamp dengan tie-breaker.

create_note_tab tidak mengganti apa pun, jadi pengecekan versi saja tidak bisa mencegah duplikat. Panggilan yang diputar ulang menjadi tab baru di versi baru. race.py create membuat 50 tab Sheet dengan 30% balasan dibuang, sehingga client melakukan retry seperti host setelah timeout:

Dengan key, retry mengembalikan hasil pertama, termasuk ID tab-nya, jadi edit_note_tab berikutnya dari agent menyasar tab yang memang ada. Itulah maksud baris "A repeated idempotency key returns the first tab" di deskripsi tool osFoundry.

Definisi singkat osFoundry tentang protokol di baliknya ada di entri glosarium MCP. Cara osFoundry menyimpan dan memulihkan kondisi Note sebelumnya dijelaskan di halaman Note versions.

#9699. How to prebake pie crust — and why you should: The key to flaky — not flabby — pie crust.

A soggy bottom. Not something you want for your baby. Or your pie crust. And while we can’t help you with your baby, there’s a simple solution to pies with soggy bottoms: prebake (also known as blind bake) the crust.

There are a number of reasons your pie can end up with a soft, pale, underbaked crust — and steps you can take to help prevent that unfortunate result.

But the one surefire way to make certain your pie’s crust will be golden brown, crisp, and delicious — just as appealing as its filling — is to prebake it. That’s right: bake the bottom crust first, before adding the filling.

Most commonly, it's smart to prebake pie crust when:

But some fillings might instead cook fully on the stovetop, like the rich, thick filling for chocolate cream pie. When it’s done, you simply pour it into its crust — and said crust had better be prebaked to perfection, since the pie’s not going anywhere near an oven.

Other pies, typically those with a more delicate, egg- and cream-based filling (think custard pie or quiche) require at least some baking — but don’t spend long enough in the oven (at a high enough temperature) to guarantee a fully baked, brown and crispy crust.

In these cases, you need to prebake your crust.

The recipe you're following may explain explicitly how to prebake your crust. But if it doesn't, follow this process:

First, roll your bottom crust and place it in the pan. Crimp or flatten the edge. Chill it for 30 minutes, to relax the gluten and firm up the fat(s); this will help prevent shrinkage, so don't skip!

Line the crust with foil, parchment, or a paper coffee filter. Fill it about two-thirds full with dried beans, uncooked rice (or other uncooked grain berries), pie weights, or granulated sugar.

Bake the crust in a preheated 375°F oven for 20 minutes, set on a baking stone or steel if you have one. Remove the crust from the oven and lift out the liner and weights. (If you’ve used sugar, save it for your future baking; it’ll be lightly toasted and yummy!)

At this point your crust is partially prebaked, and good for any of your pies that tend to exhibit a wan, flabby bottom crust when done. Think pumpkin pie: You don’t want to bake the filling so long that it’s stiff and dry, but you may pull your pie out of the oven to find your perfectly baked filling is resting in a partially baked crust. Prebaking your crust partway is a sensible solution for this scenario.

To fully prebake the crust, prick the bottom all over with a fork to prevent bubbles. Return the crust to the oven and bake for an additional 20 to 25 minutes, until it’s golden all over.

If, despite your best efforts, the lined, weighted crust still slips down the inside of the pan while it prebakes, try this: Bake the crust upside down.

To start, you’ll need two identical (or nicely nestable) pie pans with flat rims.

Place your rolled-out crust in one of the pans, anchoring it to the rim of the pan with a fork-tine crimp. Place a liner of some kind (same as above: parchment, foil, coffee filter) into the pan. Nest the second pan into the first.

Pick up both pans, turn them over, and set them on a baking sheet. Place the baking sheet and pie pans in the oven, and bake as directed above. As the crust bakes, gravity will pull it down toward its rim — rather than into a puddle at the bottom of the pan. Magic!

After 20 minutes remove the baking sheet from the oven, carefully turn the pans over, lift out the empty pan, and remove the liner. At this point, your crust is partially prebaked. To prebake it fully, place the crust back in the oven, right side up, and bake until it's golden.

If you struggle with a pale, pasty bottom crust in your fruit pie, then yes, you can prebake it — with a couple of caveats:

So, soggy bottoms begone! From now on I expect every pie you bake will have a deep golden brown, flaky, crispy crust on the bottom — all because of the prebake.

And if you have any other questions about pie — from creating tender, flaky crust to thickening fruit filling to assessing when your pie is perfectly baked — please check out our Pie Baking Guide.

#9698. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?


SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

What is SEMrush?


SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Features

  • Most accurate keyword data: Accurate keyword search volume data is crucial for SEO and PPC campaigns by allowing you to identify what keywords are most likely to bring in big sales from ad clicks. SEMrush constantly updates its databases and provides the most accurate data.
  • Largest Keyword database: SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool now features 20-billion keywords, providing marketers and SEO professionals the largest database of keywords.

  • All SEMrush users receive daily ranking data, mobile volume information, and the option to buy additional keywords by default with no additional payment or add-ons needed
  • Most accurate position tracking tool: This tool provides all subscribers with basic tracking capabilities, making it suitable for SEO professionals. Plus, the Position Tracking tool provides local-level data to everyone who uses the tool.
  • SEO Data Management: SEMrush makes managing your online data easy by allowing you to create visually appealing custom PDF reports, including Branded and White Label reports, report scheduling, and integration with GA, GMB, and GSC.
  • Toxic link monitoring and penalty recovery: With SEMrush, you can make a detailed analysis of toxic backlinks, toxic scores, toxic markers, and outreach to those sites.
  • Content Optimization and Creation Tools: SEMrush offers content optimization and creation tools that let you create SEO-friendly content. Some features include the SEO Writing Assistant, On-Page SEO Check, er/SEO Content Template, Content Audit, Post Tracking, Brand Monitoring.

Ahrefs



Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Features

  • Backlink alerts data and new keywords: Get an alert when your site is linked to or discussed in blogs, forums, comments, or when new keywords are added to a blog posting about you.
  • Intuitive interface: The intuitive design of the widget helps you see the overall health of your website and search engine ranking at a glance.
  • Site Explorer: The Site Explorer will give you an in-depth look at your site's search traffic.
  • Domain Comparison
  • Reports with charts and graphs
  • JavaScript rendering and a site audit can identify SEO issues.
  • A question explorer that provides well-crafted topic suggestions

Direct Comparisons: Ahrefs vs SEMrush

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

User Interface

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

  • You can see analytics from the dashboard, including search engine rankings to domain ratings, referring domains, and backlink
  • Jumping from one tool to another is easy. You can use the Keyword Explorer to find a keyword to target and then directly track your ranking with one click.
  • The website offers a tooltip helper tool that allows you to hover your mouse over something that isn't clear and get an in-depth explanation.

SEMRUSH



When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

You'll also find some other options like

  • A search bar allows you to enter a domain, keyword, or anything else you wish to explore.
  • A menu on the left side of the page provides quick links to relevant information, including marketing insights, projects, keyword analytics, and more.
  • The customer support resources located directly within the dashboard can be used to communicate with the support team or to learn about other resources such as webinars and blogs.
  • Detailed descriptions of every resource offered. This detail is beneficial for new marketers, who are just starting.

WHO WINS?

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

Rank Tracking

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

Ahrefs



The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRUSH



SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

All subscribers are given regular data updates and mobile search rankings upon subscribing

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

WHO WINS?

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword Research

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

  • It can search multiple keywords in a single search and analyze them together. At SEMrush, you also have this feature in Keyword Overview.
  • Ahrefs has a variety of keywords for different search engines, including Google, YouTube, Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, and other search engines.
  • When you click on a keyword, you can see its search volume and keyword difficulty, but also other keywords related to it, which you didn't use.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

The Keyword Magic Tool also lets you to:

  • Show performance metrics by keyword
  • Search results are based on both broad and exact keyword matches.
  • Show data like search volume, trends, keyword difficulty, and CPC.
  • Show the first 100 Google search results for any keyword.
  • Identify SERP Features and Questions related to each keyword
  • SEMrush has released a new Keyword Gap Tool that uncovers potentially useful keyword opportunities for you, including both paid and organic keywords.

WHO WINS?

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Competitor Analysis

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

AHREFS



Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

WHO WINS?

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

Pricing

Ahrefs

  • Lite Monthly: $99/month
  • Standard Monthly: $179/month
  • Annually Lite: $990/year
  • Annually Standard: $1790/year

SEMRUSH

  • Pro Plan: $119.95/month
  • Guru Plan:$229.95/month
  • Business Plan: $449.95/month

Which SEO tool should you choose for digital marketing?

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Consider choosing Ahrefs if you

  • Like friendly and clean interface
  • Searching for simple keyword suggestions

  • Want to get more keywords for different search engines like Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, Baidu, and more

 

Consider SEMrush if you:

  • Want more marketing and SEO features
  • Need competitor analysis tool
  • Need to keep your backlinks profile clean
  • Looking for more keyword suggestions for Google

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9693. How long does pie last in the fridge? : Because we're all wondering what to do with our apple and pumpkin pies.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions. Today: How long does pie last in the fridge?

The season of plentiful pies is upon us. When preparing several pies for a holiday meal, you may be wondering about the imminent leftovers. Should apple pie be stored differently than pumpkin pie? David from our Baker’s Hotline is here with his expert advice to help.

“Baked apple or other fruit pies can be kept covered, at room temperature, for one to two days. After that, they’ll keep in the fridge for one to two more days,” David advises. A 15-minute reheat in a 350°F oven can help revive some of that freshly baked flavor. Tent the pie with foil so it doesn’t brown further.

Interested in prepping ahead? David says that storing an assembled, ready-to-bake apple pie is a bad idea; the fruity filling will release moisture, which will make your crust soggy. Instead, roll out your pie crusts and prep your apples, but keep them separate. And wait to add the sugar and spices to the apples until you’re ready to bake the pie. This way, you can pour off any liquid that’s accumulated from the fruit without draining off your thickener, sugar, and spices.

Sliced apples turn brown, so you don’t want to keep your prepared apples in the fridge very long before baking. Aim for under 24 hours, but a squeeze of lemon juice could help them last another day or so.

And if you want to use your freezer to prep ahead, here’s how to freeze and bake fruit pies.

David advises, “Baked pumpkin pie or other pies containing eggs and/or dairy such as pecan pie, custard pie, or chiffon pie should be stored refrigerated; they’ll keep in the fridge for three to four days. I like to transfer the pie to a shallow, lidded storage container, but plastic wrap or a storage top can be used as well.”

As with apple, if you’re making your pumpkin (and other custard) pie ahead, it’s best to keep filling and crust separate. Pumpkin pie filling can be made ahead; it’ll keep, refrigerated, overnight. In fact, that's actually what we recommend doing; the custard develops incredible flavor and aroma as it sits.

If you can, serve pies the day they were made instead of refrigerating them.

Reheat refrigerated pies in a 350°F oven for about 15 minutes prior to serving.

Apple and other fruit pies will last at room temperature for up to two days, then in the fridge for two more.

Pumpkin, custard, or other egg/dairy-based pies can be stored in the fridge for up to four days.

If you’re making the crust and the filling ahead, keep them separated until it’s time to bake your pie.
